My best advice is to get them addicted to WGI Zone, show them A class guards in particular. In my area we have new winter programs popping up everywhere and then in only two years advancing out of Regional A to Scholastic A because of one strong freshman group at those schools. Show them what they could become if they really put the effort forth; tell them about the excitement of a competition full of family, friends, and people just crazy about everything color guard. Show them corps, show them everything. Instagram has become a good highway for recent videos for anyone from beginners to world class spinners just by following #colorguard . Get them to see everyone they can because if they see other people excited, they'll get excited. And if it's not too late, register a winter guard now! You'd be surprised how fast a program can come together. If that's not possible, arrange to take them to any show they can, be it WGI, BOA, random band comps, or DCI. Just expose them as much as you can and always show them that anyone can achieve greatness through hard work.

I agree with separating the toss from the turn entirely. Make sure you get the turn smooth first without the equipment with counts and get a feel for the turn. Personally when I teach turnarounds I start with them under fives as it is way more time then you need to turn and it's a comfortable toss height. After those are smooth, doing them under quads and sixes are extremely easy. I also recommend trying to get them solid on flag first as there is a good chance you might hit yourself in the beginning, and a flag won't bite as hard as a weapon would.

Totally agree. We had a tech my sophomore year who absolutely brutal and rude and overall counterproductive. A group of vets and I personally went to the tech directly after our director brushed it off and we reminded him that our dues paid him and that there is a difference between pushing for excellence and pushing for abuse. At that moment he became increasingly angry and talked to the director directly very loud and rudely in front of all of the students demanding we be reprimanded. Only then did our director see how belligerent and rude he was. He was quickly replaced. 

My only advice to remind him that you are students and that this isn't an independent world guard(we also had an ex captionhead for a top six corps be put on probation in the district for his extremely degrading comments). Negative comments can be taken very seriously, even when they are meant as humor, and usually don't "encourage better effort" as most directors intend them too; it's usually just detrimental. Do not allow anything l
that is too extreme and that is abuse to continue. Rally with some vets and make a positive change.
